t: Introduction: forensic toxicology and the aim of the session
n: In this chapter we study forensic toxicology. Impairment of health and death under the action of chemical factors are fairly common in the examination of corpses and living persons. Among violent deaths, poisonings take third place after mechanical injuries and mechanical asphyxia. Forensic medicine as a science began to take shape precisely from forensic toxicology. Topics of the chapter: the concept of poison, factors, forensic medical diagnosis, toxicokinetics, classification of poisons and individual poisonings.

Concepts of poison and poisoning. Poison is a relative concept: it is a substance that in a small amount impairs health or leads to death. Just as there is no absolute poison in nature, there is no absolutely harmless substance. According to Paracelsus, only the dose makes a given substance a medicine or a poison. Remember: a poison and poisoning are not the same thing. A poison is a substance, whereas poisoning is an impairment of health arising from the action of a small amount of it.

Branches of toxicology. Toxicology is divided into industrial, agricultural, military, food, domestic and forensic medical branches. The other types study the cause of poisoning, skilled care and prevention. Forensic toxicology solves the tasks set by law enforcement bodies in poisoning. It is also important historically: forensic medicine as a science began to take shape precisely from forensic toxicology.

Origin of poisonings. Poisoning may be homicide, suicide or an accident. According to examination data, accidents make up the majority. Suicide comes next, while homicide by poisoning is rare. In homicide and suicide the poison is administered deliberately, in an accident it is taken in by chance. Some accidental poisonings are iatrogenic: the dose of a drug is set wrongly, or another substance is used instead of one drug.

Case analysis: iatrogenic poisoning. The situation is this: during a medical procedure the drug dose was set incorrectly, or another substance was administered instead of one drug, and the patient developed signs of poisoning. Question: which does this case belong to, homicide, suicide or accident, and why? Such a case occurs by chance, that is, it belongs to the type of accident and has an iatrogenic origin. Remember: deliberate poisoning is distinguished from accidental poisoning by the presence or absence of intent in introducing the poison.

t: Four groups of factors affecting poisoning
n: The factors affecting poisoning are divided into four groups: the poison, the organism, the route of entry and external conditions. For the toxic substance, structure, quantity and solubility are important. For the organism, weight, age and state of health. For the route of entry, the speed and completeness of passage into the blood. For external conditions, temperature, humidity and a closed environment. The faster and more completely a poison passes into the blood, the stronger the toxic effect. A closed, warm, humid environment creates a predisposition to the action of alcohol and carbon monoxide.

t: Factors related to the toxic substance
n: Factors related to the toxic substance. The chemical structure of a substance determines its properties. The amount of poison is also important: in pharmacology therapeutic, toxic and lethal doses are distinguished, and liquid substances act differently depending on concentration. The state of aggregation is also significant: a gaseous substance acts more strongly than a liquid one, and a liquid more strongly than a solid, because it passes into the blood faster. Toxic action depends on solubility and stability during storage, and the action of drugs may change with time. Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide both consist of carbon and oxygen, but their toxicity is not the same.

t: Vehiculum, cumulation and influence of the medium
n: Vehiculum, cumulation and influence of the medium. The substance carrying the poison, that is, the vehiculum, may alter the degree of toxic action. A poison rarely enters in pure form: most often it is added to a drink, food and the like. The medium also plays a role. Arsenic is enhanced in an alkaline medium and weakened in an acidic one. Cyanides are enhanced in an acidic medium, whereas organophosphorus compounds are enhanced in a fatty medium. Cumulation is the accumulation of a poison in the body; it is particularly important for heavy metal compounds.

t: Quick question: factors of the toxic substance
n: Quick question: factors of the toxic substance. The question is this: barium sulphate and barium chloride are both barium salts, which of them is a strong poison and why? Answer: barium chloride is soluble in water, so it is a strong poison. Barium sulphate is insoluble and is used as a suspension in radiography of the gastrointestinal tract. About vinegar: the action of a 3% acid solution and of the essence cannot be compared. Of phenol, the concentrated form causes a local burn, the diluted form resorptive damage. Attention: with similar structure toxicity is not the same, for example carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide.

Factors related to the organism. The same amount of poison does not act equally on people of different weight; the dose of a drug is also calculated per 1 kg of weight. There is no difference by sex in toxic action, but in pregnancy women's sensitivity increases. Children are more sensitive, because their weight is small and the resistance system is not fully formed. A healthy organism resists a poison more strongly, whereas in diseases of the heart, liver and kidneys this capacity is considerably limited. When a poison enters by mouth, the composition and amount of the stomach contents may alter the action and absorption into the blood.

Genetic sensitivity, tolerance and dependence. Congenitally low cholinesterase activity enhances the action of muscle relaxants, and G6PD deficiency, that is, of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, increases sensitivity to sulphonamides. Idiosyncrasy is extreme sensitivity of the body to certain substances, and it too is explained by genetic features. Repeated exposure over a short time causes tolerance, that is, habituation; it is seen with hypnotics, analgesics and antihypertensive drugs. With narcotic and some toxic substances, psychological and physical dependence leads to a drive for larger doses. If the substance is not taken, an abstinence syndrome appears; it occurs in narcomania and toxicomania.

t: Routes of entry of poison and external conditions
n: Routes of entry of poison and external conditions. A poison enters through the skin, mouth, respiratory tract, rectum or by injection. The faster and more completely it passes into the blood, the stronger the effect. Substances insoluble in both water and fats act only locally. Organophosphorus compounds, which are highly soluble in fats, are absorbed even through intact skin. A substance absorbed from the mucosa of the respiratory tract, rectum and vagina does not pass through the liver. A closed, warm, humid environment creates a predisposition to poisoning by alcohol and carbon monoxide, whereas an open environment, low temperature and humidity weaken the effect.

t: Case analysis: poisoning in a closed environment
n: Case analysis: poisoning in a closed environment. A training example: a worker was found dead in a sewer manhole, and there was a smell of rotten eggs in the cavity of the manhole. Hydrogen sulphide is heavier than air, so it accumulates in mines, sewers and cesspits; the poisoning is usually an accident. A closed, warm, humid environment creates a predisposition to poisoning by alcohol and carbon monoxide. Question: what evidence is sought? A smell of rotten eggs from the cavities and internal organs, cherry-red blood; the air at the scene is analysed.

t: Forensic medical diagnosis of poisoning: 3 stages
n: The forensic medical diagnosis of poisoning consists of three stages. In the first stage the scene, vessels, syringe, vomit and medical documents are studied. In the second stage, on the body, injection marks, the colour of the skin and cadaveric lividity, the smell and rigor mortis are assessed. In the third stage histological, forensic chemical and other examinations are carried out; most often the forensic chemical, that is, qualitative and quantitative, examination is used. That is, diagnosis proceeds as a chain from the scene to the laboratory.

Characteristic signs on the body. Smell also gives information: in cyanide poisoning a smell of bitter almonds is perceived from the internal organs, in acetic acid a pungent specific smell. The colour of cadaveric lividity differs according to the poison: pink in carbon monoxide, bright cherry-red in cyanides, brown to brownish in poisons forming methaemoglobin, yellowish in haemolytic poisons. Rigor mortis in strychnine is rapid and strong, in chloral hydrate, curare and muscle relaxants weak and flaccid. Attention: pink lividity is typical of carbon monoxide, cherry-red of cyanides. With functional poisons there may be no characteristic signs.

t: Taking material for the laboratory: the "three points" rule
n: Taking material for the laboratory: the "three points" rule. If the poisoning substance is known, samples are taken by the three points rule: from the place where the poison entered, where it mainly acted, and from where it was eliminated from the body. Example: if the poison entered by mouth, acted on the liver and was eliminated in urine, the stomach contents, part of the liver and a whole kidney with urine are taken. If the source of the poison is unknown: 1/3 of the brain, 1/4 of the lung, 1/3 of the liver with the gallbladder and bile, and a whole kidney with urine are taken. In addition the stomach contents, one metre of intestine and 100–200 ml of blood are taken, each in a separate container. In deep putrefaction 1.5–2.0 kg of an "average sample" is taken.

Toxicokinetics is the set of processes of entry, distribution, metabolism and elimination of a poison. These four stages form a cyclic chain: entry into the body, distribution, metabolism, elimination. The quantitative aspect is related to the change in concentration: ethyl alcohol in the blood first rises, then falls. The qualitative aspect is biotransformation: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis and synthesis. These changes occur mainly in the liver.

Biotransformation, accumulation and elimination. Organophosphorus compounds become more toxic on oxidation and markedly weaker on hydrolysis. Methanol gives formaldehyde, ethanol gives acetaldehyde, ethylene glycol gives oxalic acid; the metabolites of methanol and ethylene glycol are considerably more toxic. Accumulation: fat-soluble substances in the brain, liver and adipose tissue; water-soluble ones in muscle, liver and kidneys; arsenic and lead in bone and hair. Elimination: volatile substances through the lungs, water-soluble through the kidneys, heavy metals through the large intestine, fat-soluble with bile, alcohol with saliva and milk.

Toxicodynamics is the mechanism of interaction between the poison and the organism. It is the set of reactions of the organism to the poison and its metabolites. Attention: toxicokinetics and toxicodynamics are not the same. The first shows what happens to the substance in the body, the second how the body responds to the substance. The action is conventionally divided into primary toxic, subsequent toxic and metatoxic stages. Example: the whole molecule of ethylene glycol has a narcotic effect, whereas its metabolite oxalic acid poisons the liver and kidney. Acetic acid first burns the mucosa, then haemolysis arises because of acidosis, followed by toxic hepatitis and nephrosis.

Case analysis: toxicokinetics and toxicodynamics. Situation: a person drank methyl alcohol, that is, methanol, instead of ethyl alcohol. At first brief, mild intoxication and headache were observed, then deep sleep. For several hours or even several days the condition was good; then it sharply worsened, vision was impaired, and death on day 2-3 from paralysis of the respiratory centre is possible. Question: why did the condition become severe after the latent period? Direction of the answer: methanol is oxidised more slowly than ethyl alcohol, and formaldehyde and formic acid are formed. Cardio-, nephro- and neurotoxic changes are related to formaldehyde.

t: Forensic medical classification of poisons (V.L. Popov)
n: The forensic medical classification of poisons according to V.L. Popov, in abridged form. Poisons are divided into those acting predominantly locally and those acting predominantly in general. The local ones include acids, alkalis and tincture of iodine. Of the general ones, in the destructive group are mercury, lead and arsenic; in the haemotropic group carbon monoxide, arsine and ricin; in the functional group cyanides, ethyl alcohol and strychnine. Poisons of general action are also called resorptive, since they act after absorption into the blood. Attention: local poisons also cause a general reaction, whereas with functional ones there are few morphological changes.

Corrosive substances: acids. The damaging action of an acid is exerted by free hydrogen ions: dehydrating tissue, they coagulate protein and cause coagulative, that is, dry necrosis. At the site of necrosis a dry, dense, brownish-black scab forms with inflammation around it; haemoglobin is converted into acid haematin and methaemoglobin. In the oesophagus and stomach there is severe pain and bloody vomit. In the first hours shock, asphyxia and internal bleeding may lead to death. Lethal dose: sulphuric and nitric acids 5–10 ml, hydrochloric 15–20 ml. Late death is caused by pneumonia, acute hepatorenal failure, mediastinitis or peritonitis.

t: Acids: postmortem signs and differences between types
n: Acids: postmortem signs and differences between types. Organic acids dissociate weakly: damaging with the whole molecule, they give superficial necrosis and marked inflammation. Phenol, that is, carbolic acid, is a nerve-protoplasmic poison: coma, paralysis of the respiratory centre; urine turns greenish-brown in air. With sulphuric acid the gastric mucosa is brownish-black and perforation is more often seen. With nitric acid there is a yellowish tint, a suffocating smell, toxic pulmonary oedema and pneumonia. With hydrochloric acid the mucosa is brownish-grey, and oedema of the larynx and lungs is more frequent. With acetic acid there is a sharp smell of vinegar, haemolysis and acute renal failure; its haemolytic action is stronger than that of other acids.

Alkalis and ammonia, that is, spirit of ammonia. Alkalis with hydroxyl anions liquefy proteins, saponify fats and cause colliquative necrosis. The affected area is soft, swollen and slippery; the vessels are eroded, and the blood that escapes does not clot. The lethal dose of K/Na hydroxide is 10–15 g, the local action is strong, after absorption it causes alkalosis, and the stomach wall is soft. The lethal dose of spirit of ammonia is 25–40 ml, the local action is weaker, but after absorption the CNS and respiratory centre are impaired; a smell of ammonia is perceived. It is dangerous together with alcohol.

Other corrosive substances. Formalin is a 37–40% solution of formaldehyde and may be drunk accidentally or with suicidal intent; the mucosa looks fixed. Potassium permanganate forms a brownish-reddish scab on the mucosa, and 15–20 g taken by mouth lead to death. With hydrogen peroxide the mucous membranes are whitish, foamed by gas bubbles; its 33% solution, perhydrol, in a volume of 100 ml may lead to death. Tincture of iodine and Lugol's solution leave a brown scab on the mucosa, and after absorption into the blood damage the heart, lungs, liver and kidneys.

Case analysis: corrosive substances. Situation: on the body there are streak-shaped burn marks around the mouth. The gastric mucosa is swollen, greyish-green, the wall is soft and tears easily. Question: is this the action of an acid or an alkali, and which signs support the decision? Attention: with an acid the streaks have the density of parchment, whereas with an alkali the tissue is soft, swollen and slippery. An additional key: a smell of ammonia from the internal organs indicates spirit of ammonia. With sulphuric acid the stomach is brownish-black, with nitric acid yellowish.

t: Destructive poisons: general properties and mercury
n: Destructive poisons: general properties and mercury. Mercury, lead and arsenic bind sulphydryl groups and switch off enzymes. Many accumulate, that is, cumulation occurs; mercury is found in bone and kidney even decades later. With corrosive sublimate there is "sublimate dysentery" in the large intestine and "sublimate kidney" in the kidney. With corrosive sublimate the kidneys and large intestine are severely damaged, stomatitis develops, neurotoxic action is less, the course is up to a week, acute. With organic mercury the damage is weaker, stomatitis does not develop, neurotoxic action is stronger, and the course is chronic with a latent period.

Lead, thallium and arsenic. The water-soluble salts of lead, that is, chloride, nitrate and acetate, inactivate enzymes and kill cells. Tetraethyl lead, that is, leaded petrol, enters through the skin, mouth and respiratory tract; blocking enzymes in the brain, it causes acute psychosis, convulsions and coma. Thallium salts resemble table salt, and poisoning is often an accident; gastroenteritis, ataxia, hair loss and painful polyneuropathy are seen. In arsenic poisoning, in the gastrointestinal form there is vomiting, cholera-like diarrhoea and death on day 1–2; in the paralytic form encephalopathy and coma. The lethal dose is 0.1–0.2 g. Unlike mercury, the damage to the nervous system is stronger, and anaemia develops.

Blood poisons: carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide forms stable carboxyhaemoglobin with haemoglobin; oxygen is not carried and hypoxia develops. Headache, ringing in the ears, nausea and flushing of the face appear, then coma with convulsions. Cadaveric lividity, muscles and fluid blood are pinkish-red; in the internal organs there is congestion and small haemorrhages. The first signs begin at COHb > 25-30 %, paralysis of the respiratory centre at > 60 %. In the Hoppe-Seyler test the colour does not change, and in spectroscopy 2 bands persist.

Poisons forming methaemoglobin. Nitrate, nitrite, nitrobenzene, aniline, potassium chlorate and hydroquinone form methaemoglobin; because of trivalent iron, haemoglobin cannot carry oxygen. The clinical picture is haemic hypoxia: dyspnoea, cyanosis, headache, collapse. Signs begin when methaemoglobin exceeds 30%, and above 70% death occurs. On the first day death is from haemic hypoxia, later from acute renal failure. Cadaveric lividity is bluish-brown and the blood brownish; with nitrobenzene there is a smell of bitter almonds, with aniline an aromatic smell. Methaemoglobin may not be found in the blood after 1–2 days. Nitrates act only after conversion to nitrites by intestinal microflora, so they are weaker.

Case analysis: carbon monoxide poisoning. Situation: a body was found in an enclosed room during a fire or with a faulty stove. Carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless and is formed when organic substances burn incompletely. Cadaveric lividity, muscles and fluid blood are pinkish-red; this is the colour of carboxyhaemoglobin and carboxymyoglobin. Question: carboxyhaemoglobin in the blood was negative, can carbon monoxide poisoning be excluded? Attention: no. Rapid death or being in fresh air before death lowers the result or makes it negative. The blood sample is taken as early as possible.

t: Functional poisons: those paralysing the CNS
n: Functional poisons: those paralysing the CNS. Cyanides, hydrogen sulphide and organophosphorus compounds paralyse the central nervous system. Cyanides bind the iron of cytochrome oxidase; on the body there are cherry-red lividity and a smell of bitter almonds. In a large dose cyanide causes loss of consciousness within minutes; the antidotes are substances forming methaemoglobin. Hydrogen sulphide binds cytochrome iron; there is a smell of rotten eggs and the blood is cherry-red. Organophosphorus compounds suppress cholinesterase: the pupil is constricted and rigor mortis is rapid. They are characterised by miosis, bronchospasm and bradycardia, with death from paralysis of the respiratory centre.

t: Ethyl alcohol: toxicokinetics and degrees of intoxication
n: Ethyl alcohol: toxicokinetics and degrees of intoxication. Of the alcohol, 20% is absorbed in the stomach and 80% in the intestine; 90% is metabolised by the body. Ethanol is oxidised to acetaldehyde, then to acetic acid; acetaldehyde produces the hangover syndrome. Degrees of intoxication in per mille: mild 0.5-1.5, moderate 1.5-2.5, severe 2.5-3.0, poisoning > 3.0. The Widmark constant, that is, P, indicates the fall per hour; if not determined, an average of 0.13–0.15 per mille is taken.

t: Detection and calculation of ethyl alcohol
n: Detection and calculation of ethyl alcohol. There are two tests. In the Rappoport test potassium permanganate and sulphuric acid are used, and the pink colour disappears. In the Mokhov–Shinkarenko test dichromate and sulphuric acid are used, and the yellow-orange colour turns green. They are sensitive down to 0.3–0.4 per mille; in caries and diabetes a false positive result is possible. The amount is determined by gas chromatography; the sample, blood or urine, is at least 5 ml, and the container should be full. In the resorption phase the level is higher in blood than in urine, in the elimination phase lower in blood. Widmark–Balyakin formula: A = R·r·(Ct + P·T); in men r≈0.68, in women 0.55.

t: Alcohol surrogates: methanol, ethylene glycol and others
n: Alcohol surrogates. The lethal dose of methanol is 30–100 ml: it is oxidised slowly to formaldehyde and formic acid; acidosis develops and tissue respiration is impaired. Stages: brief intoxication; a latent period from several hours to a day; then a severe condition and visual impairment, with a dilated pupil. Death is most often on day 2–3. Ethylene glycol has 4 stages: intoxication, a short latent period, CNS damage, liver and kidney damage; the metabolite is oxalic acid, and the lethal dose is 100–200 ml. Propyl, butyl and amyl alcohols lead to coma, with lethal doses of 300, 200–250 and 20–30 ml. Tetraethyl lead, 10–15 ml, causes psychosis and coma.

t: Hypnotics, strychnine, atropine and other poisons
n: Hypnotics, strychnine, atropine and other poisons. Barbiturates depress the activity of the central nervous system and increase vascular permeability. Lethal doses: barbamyl and Nembutal 1.0–2.0 g; Medinal and tetridin 3.0–5.0 g; Noxyron 5.0–10 g. Alcohol potentiates the effect, and quantitative forensic chemistry is needed. In strychnine there are tonic convulsive attacks, consciousness is preserved, and the body is arched, that is, opisthotonus; the lethal dose is 0.1–0.3 g in an adult and 0.005 g in a child. In atropine the pupil is dilated, there is delirium, and the lethal dose is 0.1 g. In pilocarpine the pupil is constricted, sweat and saliva are abundant, 0.06 g. Pachycarpine 1.0–2.0 g; clonidine 0.005–0.01 g. The signs are deep sleep, fall of pressure and temperature, coma; death is from paralysis of the respiratory centre.

Quick question: functional poisons. Question: functional poisons usually do not cause marked morphological changes in the internal organs, so on what does the diagnosis rest? Answer: on the circumstances of the event, the clinical picture of poisoning, and the results of toxicological and other laboratory examinations. Rigor mortis in strychnine is rapid and strong, in chloral hydrate, curare and muscle relaxants weak and flaccid. Attention: in cyanide poisoning cadaveric lividity is bright cherry-red, in carbon monoxide pink. Do not swap the colours.

t: Poisoning by narcotic and psychotropic substances
n: Poisoning by narcotic and psychotropic substances. Opiates and cannabis are sedative, cocaine and amphetamine stimulant. Death from opiates occurs from paralysis of the respiratory centre. Death associated with narcotics may be poisoning, suicide, accident or homicide. With repeated use dependence, tolerance and abstinence are seen; postmortem signs fall into 4 groups, and they are only indirect evidence. Detection in urine: cannabinoids begin at 1-3 hours and last 24-168 hours, heroin begins at 2-6 hours and lasts 24-72 hours, cocaine 2-6 hours and 48-72 hours, phencyclidine 4-6 hours and 7-14 days.

Food poisoning. Food poisoning is usually an accident; if a poison is added to prepared food from outside, it does not belong here. Toxic infections include salmonella, Escherichia coli and gastroenterocolitis. Intoxications include botulism and staphylococcal toxin. Among plants and fungi are the death cap, false morel and water hemlock; among animal products and additives the neurotoxin of fish roe and heliotrope-contaminated grain. Botulism is an anaerobic toxin and occurs in canned food; death is usually on the second day from paralysis of the respiratory centre. In death from bacterial poisoning, if the diagnosis is confirmed, a pathological anatomical examination is carried out, otherwise a forensic medical examination.

t: Importance of laboratory examinations and conclusion
n: Importance of laboratory examinations and conclusion. Laboratory examinations are important in proving or excluding poisoning. A false positive result may arise from use as a drug, putrefaction, occupational contact or an error in collection. Samples are taken as quickly as possible: blood, urine, gastric lavage, vomit, faeces, residue of the poison or its container. The results are always assessed critically, together with the circumstances of the event, clinical or catamnestic data and the macroscopic examination of the body. Most often forensic chemical and histological examinations are carried out; histology reveals microscopic changes.
